TASK: READ AND ANSWER

Below is a short note. Read it, and answer the questions using only what it says. Do not use anything you know from elsewhere beyond the one background fact each question names.

1. A reader who already knows USAFacts' guide to AI-ready data reads this note. Does the note let that reader learn what this work did with the guide: which of the four qualities it kept, what it added, what became measurable, and what did not? Answer and name anything they could not learn.
2. Name every term on the page that a chief information officer new to the term SI would not already know. List each such term, or say none.

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
{"q1": "...", "q2": "..."}

NOTE
Prepared 15 October 2026.

The data nonprofit USAFacts set out four qualities that public data should have if the SI systems now reading it are to use it well: that it be accessible, understandable, accurate, and open. This work keeps those four qualities as the backbone of its readiness framework, each one a top-level heading left as USAFacts wrote it, under which the detailed measures hang.

To those four it added three areas the guide does not cover: a standing loop that tests and re-tests how well SI systems read the data, the practice of treating every data release the way careful software teams treat a deployment, and a set of concerns particular to official statistics, such as whether a margin of error still travels with a figure once a machine restates it. Each added area rests on named, published standards rather than on assertion, among them the national framework for managing the risks of these systems, open standards for data contracts and software supply chains, and the catalog, exchange, and data-quality standards of the statistical community, alongside USAFacts' own later guidance. Many of the four qualities became tests a machine can run against an agency's website today, with no permission and no paid tools: whether the data is offered in a machine format, whether a documented machine interface and a full download exist, whether crawlers are allowed to reach it, whether it is listed for discovery and described in structured markup, whether it carries a machine-readable release date and a machine-readable licence, whether it is entered in a public inventory, and whether a plain account of how it was made can be reached from the data page. One of the four did not become such a test: accuracy asks whether a system that reads the data restates it correctly, which can be judged only by putting questions to each product and scoring the answers, not by reading a website, so it waits on funded tooling. A few finer points of the other qualities could not be made into a runnable test at all, for want of a settled method or a public signal to read, and these are marked plainly as open gaps rather than scored.

The result is that every test the public tier runs traces back to one of the framework's qualities or added areas, so a machine's real experience of an agency's website can be read in the very terms USAFacts set out, and measured the same way for all 16 federal statistical agencies.

## Sources

1. Standards for Excellent Data Products: Detailed User Guide (Federal Data Excellence). USAFacts, Partnership for Public Service, 2026. <https://media.usafacts.org/m/260cbbd653fb33ec/original/Detailed-User-Guide-Federal-Data-Excellence-Standards.pdf>
2. AI-Ready Data: Ensuring Public Data Meets the Needs of AI and the American Public: The USAFacts Guide to AI-Ready Data for Government Agencies. USAFacts, 2026. <https://media.usafacts.org/m/634ac133d72ded81/original/USAFacts_AIReadinessForGovernment.pdf>
3. NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF). NIST, n.d. <https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1>
4. Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS): Definition. Bitol (Linux Foundation AI & Data), 2026. <https://bitol-io.github.io/open-data-contract-standard/latest/>
5. SLSA Specification v1.0 (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts). OpenSSF SLSA project, 2023. <https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/>
6. Data Catalog Vocabulary (DCAT) - Version 3 (W3C Recommendation). W3C Dataset Exchange Working Group, 2024. <https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-dcat-3/>
7. SDMX 3.0 Technical Specifications, Section 1: Framework for SDMX Technical Standards. SDMX Technical Working Group, 2021. <https://sdmx.org/wp-content/uploads/SDMX_3-0-0_SECTION_1_FINAL-1_0.pdf>
8. FCSM 25-03: AI-Ready Federal Statistical Data: An Extension of Communicating Data Quality. Federal Committee on Statistical Methodology (FCSM), 2025. <https://statspolicy.gov/assets/fcsm/files/docs/FCSM.25.03_AI-Ready-Extension-Data-Quality.pdf>

Derived from the project's readiness framework record and the current published public-tier grid, measured across all 16 federal statistical agencies in September and October 2026. The detailed report and the connected store hold the evidence behind each check.
